matching.reasoningTemplate: 'Stones, bones, groans, moans' with known malignancy suggests hypercalcaemia.

clinicalPearls: Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to ~20% of cancer patients; the typical picture is a patient with known malignancy found hypercalcaemic on routine labs, though occasionally hypercalcaemia is the presenting feature of an undiagnosed cancer (p.737).
Most malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia runs a relatively acute course, in contrast to the chronic, fluctuating high-normal pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism or occasionally myeloma (p.363).
An elevated PTHrP level confirms HHM and is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcaemic cancer patients; PTH should be suppressed in true HHM (p.738).
Features favouring HHM over primary hyperparathyroidism: known malignancy, recent onset, and very high serum calcium levels (p.738).
PTHrP shares homology with the first ~13 amino acids of PTH and binds the PTH receptor, explaining the PTH-like biochemical effects on bone and kidney (p.363, 737).
Serum free light chains should be checked when myeloma is suspected, since ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (p.364).

Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is one of the few clinical settings where measuring serum 1,25(OH)2D is genuinely useful — it is elevated or inappropriately normal in lymphoma- and granulomatous-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.364).
Always confirm true hypercalcaemia first by correcting for albumin (add ~0.8 mg/dL to total calcium per 1.0 g/dL fall in albumin below 4.0 g/dL) to exclude pseudohypercalcaemia (p.363).
harrison.pathophysiology: Calcium balance is governed by PTH and the vitamin D metabolites 1,25(OH)2D and 25(OH)D acting across parathyroid, kidney, intestine and bone. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy arises mainly through three mechanisms. (1) PTHrP overproduction by solid tumours (squamous head/neck, lung, skin; breast; genitourinary; gastrointestinal) — PTHrP mimics PTH at the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. (2) Local osteolysis from skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma), where metastatic deposits secrete PTHrP and chemokines driving bone breakdown. (3) Excess 1,25(OH)2D production, notably by lymphomas (and granulomatous disease) via macrophage CYP27B1 converting 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. PTHrP induction is linked to PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli signalling, TGF-beta, oncogene activation (e.g. Ras) and p53 loss. In all these malignant mechanisms, the high serum calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR and appropriately suppresses endogenous PTH (p.363, 737).
additionalDifferentials: Primary hyperparathyroidism (the other most common cause of hypercalcaemia; chronic, often with low/low-normal phosphate and inappropriately normal/high PTH) (p.362-364)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) — autosomal dominant, inactivating CASR mutations; calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01, parathyroid surgery ineffective (p.363)
Multiple myeloma (consider in malignant setting; can also cause chronic hypercalcaemia) (p.363-364)
Granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, leprosy, fungal infection, foreign-body reaction) via extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D (p.362-363)
Vitamin D intoxication (excess 25(OH)D or 1,25(OH)2D; CYP24A1 deficiency) (p.362-363)
Thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, prolonged immobilisation (increased bone resorption) (p.363)
Milk-alkali syndrome / excess calcium intake or TPN (p.362-363)
Drugs: thiazides, vitamin A, lithium, foscarnet, teriparatide, aromatase inhibitors; rebound resorption after denosumab discontinuation (p.362)
Endocrine causes: adrenal insufficiency, phaeochromocytoma, acromegaly, VIPoma (p.362)
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism; rare ectopic PTH secretion (p.362-363)
infectionMimics: Tuberculosis — can cause hypercalcaemia through granulomatous extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production, mimicking a malignant cause (p.362-363)
Other granulomatous infections (leprosy, fungal infections) via the same macrophage CYP27B1 mechanism (p.362-363)
nonInfectiousMimics: Primary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism — PTH-driven hypercalcaemia mimicking malignant hypercalcaemia (p.362-364)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia — benign mimic where surgery is ineffective (p.363)
Sarcoidosis and other non-infectious granulomatous/foreign-body reactions (p.362-363)
Pseudohypercalcaemia (e.g. calcium-binding IgM in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, or spuriously high reading from altered albumin binding) (p.362-363)
additionalInvestigations: Intact PTH by two-site assay — the key second test; suppressed in HHM, inappropriately normal/elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism (p.363-364)
PTHrP level — to confirm hypercalcaemia of malignancy when needed (p.364, 738)
Serum phosphate — low/hypophosphataemia with PTHrP and primary hyperparathyroidism; high-normal/elevated with vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.363-364, 738)
Serum 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D — 1,25(OH)2D raised/inappropriately normal in lymphoma and granulomatous causes (p.364)
Serum free light chains plus protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to evaluate for myeloma (p.364)
Urinary calcium / calcium-creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01 suggests FHH; >0.02 fractional excretion supports pHPT) (p.363)
Genetic testing (CASR, GNA11, AP2S1) if FHH suspected and urine studies inconclusive (p.363)
ECG — may show shortened QTc/ST segments, bradyarrhythmias, AV block, QRS widening, bundle branch block (p.364, 738)
redFlags: Markedly elevated calcium (>14 mg/dL / >3.5 mmol/L) with progressive lethargy, stupor or coma (p.363-364, 737)
Severe GI involvement — nausea, vomiting, anorexia, peptic ulcer or pancreatitis (p.364)
Acute renal failure and volume depletion from hypercalcaemia-induced nephrogenic concentrating defect and polyuria (p.364)
Cardiac conduction abnormalities — bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc (p.364)
pitfalls: Failing to correct calcium for albumin can produce pseudohypercalcaemia or pseudohypocalcaemia and a false diagnosis (p.363).
FHH may present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcaemia and be mistaken for primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid surgery is ineffective in FHH and must be excluded (p.363).
Mild hypercalcaemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is often asymptomatic or causes only vague neuropsychiatric or constitutional symptoms, so it may be overlooked (p.363).
Ionised calcium measurement is easily distorted by collection technique (e.g. prolonged tourniquet); corrected total calcium is generally preferable (p.363).
Up to ~3% of myeloma is undetected by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — check free light chains (p.364).
In immobilisation-related hypercalcaemia, an unrecognised underlying driver (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may coexist and should be sought, especially in older patients (p.363).
harrison.severityClassification: By total serum calcium: mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (often asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor or coma, prominent GI symptoms and acute renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.363-364).
